chunks: And from him, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Sama'ah, from Abd al-Hamid, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:
"The leper (one with leprosy), the blind, and the lame are returned [in marriage]."
As for the one who is branded (with stoning punishment), a man is not entitled to return her; he has heard that from her private part.
And that the dowry is upon the one who married her off.
And the dowry became his responsibility because he deceived her.
And if a man married a woman, or married her off to a man, who did not know the inner details of her affair, there is nothing upon him [to pay], and he takes the dowry from her.

key_terms.الْبَرْصَاءُ: The leper (one with leprosy), a specific physical defect
key_terms.الْعَرْجَاءُ: The lame woman, a specific physical defect
key_terms.الْعَمْيَاءُ: The blind woman, a specific physical defect
key_terms.الْمَحْدُودَةُ: The branded woman (one who received stoning punishment), considered a distinct category
key_terms.دَخِيلَةَ أَمْرِهَا: The inner details/hidden affairs of her
key_terms.رَدُّ: Return (of a spouse due to a hidden defect)

ai.seo_question: What are the hidden defects that allow a spouse to be returned in Shia Islamic jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the jurisprudence of 'rad al-mar'ah' (returning a wife due to hidden defects), distinguishing between physical impairments like leprosy and blindness, which warrant return, and branding, which may not if the defect is external or known. It establishes the principle of 'tadlis' (concealment) to determine liability for the dowry (mahr), assigning it to the arranger who concealed the defect, while exempting them if the defect was genuinely unknown. This ruling underscores the Shia emphasis on transparency in marriage contracts and the protection of the wife's rights against deceptive practices by matchmakers or parents.
